lessons.title: Feedlot layout and bunk management
lessons.body: A well-designed feedlot saves you labour, reduces waste, and keeps cattle healthy. Start with the pen: allow 15â20 square metres per animal for a 450 kg steer, with a 2â3% slope for drainage. In hot African climates, orient pens east-west so cattle get shade during the hottest part of the day. Provide at least 3 metres of shade per animal if you have trees or shade cloth. The feed bunk should be on the highest, driest part of the pen, with a concrete apron 2.5â3 metres wide to prevent mud. Allow 30â45 cm of bunk space per head so all cattle can eat at once. A common mistake is too little bunk space, which causes aggressive feeding and acidosis. Water troughs must be clean and provide 40â60 litres per head per day; place them opposite the bunk to encourage exercise. Bunk management means keeping feed fresh and consistent. Feed twice daily at the same times, e.g., 7 am and 3 pm. Clean out old feed before adding new. Use a feed bunk reader or simply a stick to measure how much feed is left before the next feeding. The goal is 0â5% orts (leftover feed) on a dry matter basis. If you find more than 10% orts, reduce the next feed by 5â10%. If the bunk is empty, increase by 5%. Never let the bunk stay empty for more than an hour, as this causes hunger and gorging. For small-scale feedlots in Africa, a simple two-row bunk with a central alley works well. Use locally available materials like treated poles and galvanised sheets, but ensure no sharp edges. Keep the area around the bunk clean to avoid attracting rodents and birds, which spread disease.

lessons.title: Step-up and step-down feeding programs
lessons.body: When cattle first arrive at the feedlot, their rumen is not used to high-grain diets. You must adapt them slowly over 21â28 days using a step-up program. Start with a receiving diet of 40â50% roughage (e.g., maize stover, hay) and 50â60% concentrate. Feed this for the first 3â5 days. Then increase concentrate by 10â15% every 3â4 days. For example: Day 1â4: 50% concentrate; Day 5â8: 60%; Day 9â12: 70%; Day 13â16: 80%; Day 17â21: 85â90%. By day 21â28, cattle should be on the finishing diet (85â90% concentrate). Always provide long-stem roughage (e.g., 0.5â1 kg per head per day) during the step-up to stimulate chewing and saliva production. Watch for signs of acidosis: loose manure, reduced feed intake, or cattle kicking at their belly. If these appear, hold the concentrate level for a few days. Step-down feeding is used when cattle are sold or when you need to reduce feed costs. For example, if maize prices rise, you can step down the concentrate by 5% every 3 days, replacing it with roughage, but never drop below 50% concentrate for growing cattle. In Africa, where feed quality varies, test your roughage and concentrate for protein and energy. A simple rule: for every 10% increase in concentrate, add 0.5% calcium and 0.3% salt to the diet to prevent urinary calculi. Use a feed mixer wagon or mix by hand in small operations. Weigh ingredients accuratelyâa 10% error in concentrate can cause acidosis. Keep records of each step to know what works for your herd.

lessons.title: Monitoring feed intake and performance
lessons.body: To make money in a feedlot, you must know how much feed your cattle eat and how well they grow. Dry matter intake (DMI) is the key number. For a 300 kg steer gaining 1.2 kg per day, expect DMI of 2.5â3% of body weight, i.e., 7.5â9 kg of dry matter per day. For a 450 kg steer gaining 1.5 kg per day, DMI is 2.2â2.5% of body weight, i.e., 10â11 kg per day. Measure feed offered and feed left over (orts) daily. Subtract orts from offered to get actual intake. Use a scale to weigh feedâdo not guess. For small feedlots, a hanging scale or platform scale works. Record daily feed intake per pen. If intake drops by more than 10% from the previous day, check for acidosis, bloat, or water problems. Weigh cattle every 28 days. Use a livestock scale or weigh tape. Calculate average daily gain (ADG): (final weight â initial weight) Ã· number of days. For example, if a steer goes from 300 kg to 384 kg in 70 days, ADG = 84 Ã· 70 = 1.2 kg per day. Feed conversion ratio (FCR) = feed intake Ã· weight gain. A good FCR is 5:1 to 7:1 on a dry matter basis. If FCR is above 8:1, your diet is too expensive or cattle are sick. In Africa, use a simple notebook or smartphone app like FarmTrack or Livestock Manager to record data. Also monitor manure: loose manure means too much concentrate; dry, firm manure means too little. Check water intake: cattle drink 3â5 litres per kg of dry matter intake. If water intake drops, intake will drop. Finally, calculate cost per kg of gain: total feed cost Ã· total weight gain. This tells you if your feeding strategy is profitable.

lessons.title: Managing acidosis and bloat
lessons.body: Acidosis and bloat are the two biggest killers in feedlots. Acidosis happens when cattle eat too much grain too fast. The rumen pH drops below 5.5, killing good bacteria and causing inflammation. Signs: loose, grey manure, reduced feed intake, cattle kicking at their belly, and in severe cases, staggering and death. To prevent acidosis, follow the step-up program strictly. Never increase concentrate by more than 10% every 3 days. Add buffers like sodium bicarbonate at 0.5â1% of the diet, or magnesium oxide at 0.2â0.4%. Provide long-stem roughage (e.g., 0.5â1 kg per head per day) to stimulate chewing and saliva, which naturally buffers the rumen. If acidosis occurs, remove all concentrate for 24 hours and feed only hay. Then reintroduce concentrate slowly. For bloat, which is gas trapped in the rumen, signs include a swollen left side, laboured breathing, and drooling. Bloat is often caused by lush legumes like alfalfa or clover, or by high-grain diets with too little fibre. Prevent bloat by limiting legume hay to 20% of the diet, or by feeding poloxalene (Bloat Guard) at 2â4 g per 100 kg body weight per day. In Africa, where alfalfa is expensive, use grass hay and add 10% molasses to improve palatability. If an animal bloats, walk it briskly for 10â15 minutes. If that fails, use a stomach tube to release gas. In severe cases, a vet may need to trocarise (puncture the rumen). Always have a vetâs number on hand. Keep a first-aid kit with sodium bicarbonate, mineral oil, and a stomach tube. Record every case to identify problem pens or feeds.

lessons.title: Feed delivery and weighing accuracy
lessons.body: Accurate feed delivery is the difference between profit and loss. A 5% error in feed weighing can cost you 5% of your feed budget. For a 100-head feedlot eating 10 kg per head per day, that is 50 kg of feed wasted or underfed daily. Use a calibrated scale. For total mixed rations (TMR), a feed mixer wagon with a scale is ideal, but for small-scale operations, a platform scale or hanging scale works. Weigh each ingredient separately. For example, if the diet is 70% maize, 20% soybean meal, 5% molasses, and 5% minerals, weigh 70 kg maize, 20 kg soybean, 5 kg molasses, and 5 kg minerals for a 100 kg batch. Mix thoroughly for at least 5 minutes. If mixing by hand, mix on a concrete floor with a shovel, turning the pile three times. Deliver feed at the same time each day. Use a feed cart or wheelbarrow. Distribute feed evenly along the bunk so all cattle have equal access. Do not dump feed in one spot. After feeding, check for leftover feed (orts). If orts are more than 5%, reduce the next feeding by the same amount. Weigh orts to know exactly how much. Clean the scale weekly and check zero. For accuracy, use a scale with 0.5 kg increments. In Africa, many feedlots use a simple beam scale or a digital luggage scale for small batches. Always calibrate with a known weight, like a 20 kg bag of cement. Keep a log of feed delivered per pen. If a pen consistently has high orts, check the dietâmaybe it is too fine or too dusty. If a pen has no orts, they may be hungryâincrease feed by 5%. Never guess; weigh everything.

lessons.title: Record keeping and data analysis for feedlot efficiency
lessons.body: You cannot improve what you do not measure. Record keeping is the backbone of a profitable feedlot. Start with a simple notebook or a spreadsheet on a phone or computer. For each pen, record daily: date, feed offered (kg), feed refused (orts, kg), number of cattle, and any health issues. Weekly, record cattle weights (or weigh a sample of 10 cattle). Monthly, calculate key performance indicators (KPIs): average daily gain (ADG), dry matter intake (DMI), feed conversion ratio (FCR), and cost per kg of gain. For example, if a pen of 20 steers eats 200 kg of feed per day (10 kg per head) and gains 24 kg per day (1.2 kg per head), FCR = 200 Ã· 24 = 8.3:1. If your target is 6:1, you need to improve. Analyse data by pen, by diet, and by season. In Africa, rainy seasons may reduce intake due to mud; dry seasons may increase dust and reduce intake. Use records to adjust feeding times or add water to reduce dust. Calculate break-even price: total costs (feed, labour, health, bedding) Ã· total weight gain. If break-even is 2.50 USD per kg and market price is 2.80 USD, you make a profit. Use simple software like Excel or free apps like Feedlot Manager or Herdwatch. For small-scale farmers, a wall chart with daily feed and weekly weights works. Review records every week with your team. Identify pens with low ADG or high FCR and investigate: is it the diet, disease, or bunk management? Keep records for at least 3 years to see trends. Finally, use records to negotiate better prices for feed and cattle. Data is power.

lessons.title: Practical Reference
lessons.body:
Practical Reference: Feedlot Management and Feeding Strategies

In African feedlots â from the Highveld of South Africa to the peri-urban fattening units of Kenya, Zambia and Botswana â margin is made or lost in the bunk. Feed represents 70â85% of the cost of gain, so every kilogram of feed delivered must convert into saleable liveweight. This practical reference consolidates the operational essentials of feedlot layout, bunk management, step-up/step-down programmes, intake monitoring, acidosis control, feed delivery accuracy and record keeping into a single working document for feedlot managers, nutritionists and pen riders.

The guiding business principle is simple: measure, then manage. Feedlots that weigh every load, record every refusal and review close-out data per pen consistently outperform those that run on intuition. In African markets where feed grain and protein concentrate prices are volatile, the difference between a 6:1 and a 7:1 feed conversion ratio can be the difference between profit and loss.

Feedlot Layout and Bunk Management

A functional feedlot layout separates traffic flows: incoming cattle, feed delivery, manure removal and outgoing slaughter cattle should never cross unnecessarily. The feed alley must be wide enough for a mixer wagon or tractor-drawn feed buggy to travel in one direction, with a turning bay at each end. Bunk height and reach-over design determine how easily cattle access feed and how much is wasted.

Bunk space per animal depends on body weight and feeding frequency. As a rule of thumb, allow 250â300 mm of linear bunk space per head for cattle up to 300 kg, and 300â400 mm for heavier cattle. Under-feeding at the bunk creates competition, increases variation in intake and slows compensatory gain. Over-allocation wastes feed and encourages sorting.

Step-Up and Step-Down Feeding Programmes

Newly received cattle must be adapted from a high-forage receiving diet to a high-concentrate finishing diet. This is achieved through a step-up programme, typically over 14â28 days depending on the starting weight, prior nutrition and health status. Each step increases concentrate by 5â10 percentage points while reducing roughage. The objective is to allow rumen papillae and microbial populations to adapt without triggering acidosis.

A step-down programme is used when cattle are sold, when feed quality changes, or when acidosis risk escalates. It involves reversing the concentrate:roughage ratio to stabilise rumen function before resuming the step-up. Step-down is also used during heat stress events, when intake naturally drops and a more fibrous diet reduces metabolic heat load.

In African feedlots where roughage such as maize stover, wheat straw or hay is locally available, the step-up can be economically advantageous because it uses cheaper fibre early in the feeding period. However, if roughage is scarce or expensive, a shorter step-up with careful bunk management may be justified â but only where the manager can monitor intake daily.

Monitoring Feed Intake and Performance

Daily dry matter intake (DMI) is the single most useful early-warning indicator in a feedlot. A drop in intake across a pen â even 10% â can signal acidosis, heat stress, water failure, or a feed delivery error. Conversely, a sudden increase in intake may indicate under-feeding the previous day or a bunk-reading error.

Performance should be tracked per pen, not just per feedlot. Key metrics include average daily gain (ADG), feed conversion ratio (FCR), cost of gain, days on feed, and close-out margin. In African feedlots, where cattle are often sourced from communal or smallholder systems with variable genetics, ADG can range from 0.8 kg/day to 1.6 kg/day. FCR typically ranges from 5.5:1 to 8:1 depending on diet energy density and cattle type.

Table 2: Benchmark performance indicators for African feedlots (finishing steers)

Source: Compiled from FAO livestock production data, South African Feedlot Association (SAFA) industry reports, and ILRI feedlot research in East Africa. Benchmarks vary by breed, starting weight and diet.

Managing Acidosis and Bloat

Acidosis occurs when rumen pH drops below 5.6 for extended periods, usually because of rapid fermentation of starch from grain. Sub-acute ruminal acidosis (SARA) is more common and more costly than acute acidosis because it depresses intake and fibre digestion without obvious symptoms. Bloat is a separate but related condition, often triggered by frothy legume-rich diets or sudden changes in feed.

Control measures include gradual step-up, adequate effective fibre, ionophores (where registered), buffering agents (sodium bicarbonate), consistent feeding times, and avoiding sudden changes in feed ingredient or particle size. In African feedlots where maize meal, hominy chop, molasses and brewers' grain are common energy sources, the risk of rapid starch fermentation is high and step-up discipline is non-negotiable.

â  SAFETY WARNING â ACIDOSIS AND BLOAT EMERGENCY

Acute acidosis and bloat can kill cattle within hours. If you observe staggering, laboured breathing, profuse diarrhoea, or a distended left flank, act immediately: remove all concentrate from the bunk, provide long-stem roughage and fresh water, and contact a veterinarian. Never attempt to relieve bloat by inserting a trocar unless trained and authorised â incorrect placement can cause fatal peritonitis. Do not increase concentrate in the diet until all affected animals have recovered and intake has stabilised for at least 48 hours.

Feed Delivery and Weighing Accuracy

Feed delivery errors are a hidden profit leak. A 5% over-delivery on a 10,000-tonne annual feed budget is 500 tonnes of wasted feed â often more than the entire net margin of a medium-sized African feedlot. Weighing accuracy depends on scale calibration, loader operator discipline, and mixer wagon condition.

Best practice includes:

  • Calibrate feed scales monthly and after any major repair.
  • Verify mixer wagon accuracy by weighing a known load of a single ingredient.
  • Record actual delivered weight versus target for every load.
  • Inspect bunks before feeding â never feed on top of stale or spoiled feed.
  • Keep a bunk-reading log with a consistent 0â4 scale (0 = empty, 4 = full).

In many African feedlots, feed is delivered by tractor-drawn mixer wagons or by hand. Hand-feeding increases risk of inconsistency; where possible, invest in a weigh box or load cells on the wagon. The payback period is often less than one year through reduced over-feeding alone.

Record Keeping and Data Analysis for Feedlot Efficiency

Records are the foundation of feedlot profitability. At minimum, a feedlot should maintain:

  • Pen-level daily feed delivery and refusal records.
  • Individual or pen-level entry weight, exit weight and days on feed.
  • Health treatment records (animal ID, date, product, dose, withdrawal period).
  • Feed ingredient receipts, batch numbers and nutrient analyses.
  • Close-out summaries per pen: ADG, FCR, cost of gain, mortality, margin.

Data analysis should be routine, not annual. Weekly review of intake and bunk scores allows early correction. Monthly review of close-out data identifies systemic issues â for example, a pen that consistently underperforms may indicate poor cattle sourcing, inadequate bunk space, or a health challenge. In African contexts where record-keeping may be paper-based, a simple notebook or spreadsheet is sufficient if used consistently.

Quick Reference Checklist

  1. Bunk space: 250â400 mm per head depending on weight and feeding frequency.
  2. Step-up: 14â28 days, increasing concentrate by 5â10 percentage points per step.
  3. Daily intake check: Investigate any pen-level drop greater than 10%.
  4. Acidosis watch: Loose dung, reduced intake, laminitis â act before it spreads.
  5. Scale calibration: Monthly, and after any repair or ingredient change.
  6. Bunk reading: Use a consistent 0â4 scale before every feeding.
  7. Close-out records: Calculate ADG, FCR and cost of gain per pen.
  8. Water: Ensure adequate trough space and flow rate â water drives intake.

Further Reading (Free Official Sources)

  • Meat & Livestock Australia â Feedlot Research and Development
  • ILRI â Feedlot and Livestock Feeding Research in East Africa
  • South African Feedlot Association (SAFA) â Industry Resources
  • WOAH â Terrestrial Animal Health Code (feed and feeding sections)

quiz.q: What is the recommended bunk space per head for feedlot cattle?
quiz.explanation: 30â45 cm of bunk space per head allows all cattle to eat at once, reducing aggression and acidosis risk.

quiz.q: What is the ideal percentage of orts (leftover feed) in the bunk before the next feeding?
quiz.explanation: A small amount of orts (0â5%) indicates cattle are eating well without overfeeding.

quiz.q: How often should you increase concentrate during a step-up program?
quiz.explanation: Increasing concentrate by 10â15% every 3â4 days allows the rumen to adapt without causing acidosis.

quiz.q: What is the typical length of a step-up feeding program?
quiz.explanation: A 21â28 day step-up program is standard to adapt cattle to a high-concentrate finishing diet.

quiz.q: Which mineral should be added to prevent urinary calculi when increasing concentrate?
quiz.explanation: Adding 0.5% calcium helps balance the high phosphorus in grains and prevents urinary calculi.

quiz.q: What is the expected dry matter intake for a 300 kg steer gaining 1.2 kg per day?
quiz.explanation: DMI is 2.5â3% of body weight, so for 300 kg, that is 7.5â9 kg of dry matter per day.

quiz.q: What does a feed conversion ratio (FCR) of 8:1 mean?
options: A) 8 kg of feed per kg of gain
B) 8 kg of gain per kg of feed
quiz.explanation: FCR is feed intake divided by weight gain, so 8:1 means 8 kg of feed produces 1 kg of gain.

quiz.q: How often should you weigh cattle to monitor performance?
quiz.explanation: Weighing every 28 days gives a reliable average daily gain without causing too much stress.

quiz.q: What is a sign of acidosis in feedlot cattle?
quiz.explanation: Loose, grey manure is a classic sign of rumen acidosis due to too much grain.

quiz.q: What is the recommended inclusion rate of sodium bicarbonate to prevent acidosis?
quiz.explanation: Sodium bicarbonate at 0.5â1% of the diet helps buffer rumen pH and prevent acidosis.

quiz.q: Which feed is most likely to cause bloat?
quiz.explanation: Lush legumes like alfalfa are high in soluble protein and can cause frothy bloat.

quiz.q: What is the first step if an animal shows signs of bloat?
quiz.explanation: Walking briskly helps stimulate rumen motility and can help expel gas.

quiz.q: What is the recommended amount of long-stem roughage during step-up?
options: A) 0.1 kg per head per day
B) 0.5â1 kg per head per day
C) 5â10 kg per head per day
quiz.explanation: 0.5â1 kg of long-stem roughage per head per day stimulates chewing and saliva production.

quiz.q: Why is accurate weighing of feed ingredients important?
options: B) It prevents acidosis and saves money
C) It makes feed more palatable
quiz.explanation: A 5% error in weighing can cause acidosis or waste money on overfeeding.

quiz.q: How long should you mix a total mixed ration (TMR) after adding all ingredients?
quiz.explanation: Mixing for at least 5 minutes ensures a uniform diet and prevents sorting.

quiz.q: What should you do if a pen has no orts (empty bunk)?
quiz.explanation: An empty bunk means cattle are hungry; increase feed by 5% to meet their needs.

quiz.q: What is the recommended frequency for cleaning and calibrating a feed scale?
quiz.explanation: Weekly cleaning and calibration ensure accurate feed delivery and prevent drift.

quiz.q: Which of the following is a key performance indicator (KPI) for feedlot efficiency?
quiz.explanation: Average daily gain (ADG) measures growth performance and is a core KPI.

quiz.q: How is feed conversion ratio (FCR) calculated?
options: A) Weight gain Ã· feed intake
B) Feed intake Ã· weight gain
C) Feed cost Ã· weight gain
D) Weight gain Ã· days on feed
quiz.explanation: FCR = total feed intake divided by total weight gain, expressed as a ratio.

quiz.q: What does a break-even price represent?
options: A) The price you sell cattle for
B) The cost per kg of gain
D) The feed cost per day
quiz.explanation: Break-even price is total costs divided by total weight gain, the minimum price needed to cover costs.

quiz.q: Why should you keep feedlot records for at least 3 years?
options: A) To see long-term trends and improve decisions
B) Because it is required by law
C) To sell to other farmers
quiz.explanation: Long-term records help identify seasonal patterns and make better management decisions.

quiz.q: What is the recommended shade allowance per animal in hot climates?
quiz.explanation: At least 3 mÂ² of shade per animal reduces heat stress and maintains feed intake.

quiz.q: What is the ideal slope for a feedlot pen?
quiz.explanation: A 2â3% slope allows proper drainage without causing erosion or mud.

quiz.q: How much water does a feedlot steer typically drink per day?
quiz.explanation: A 450 kg steer drinks 40â60 litres per day, depending on temperature and diet.

quiz.q: What is the first step when acidosis is suspected in a pen?
options: B) Remove all concentrate for 24 hours
quiz.explanation: Removing concentrate and feeding only hay helps the rumen recover from acidosis.

quiz.q: Which of the following is a good source of long-stem roughage in Africa?
quiz.explanation: Maize stover is a locally available, affordable long-stem roughage that stimulates chewing.

quiz.q: What is the purpose of a feed bunk reader or stick?
options: A) To measure feed depth and estimate orts
quiz.explanation: A bunk reader helps estimate how much feed is left, guiding the next feeding amount.

quiz.q: What is the recommended concentrate level in a finishing diet?
quiz.explanation: A finishing diet typically contains 85â90% concentrate for maximum energy and gain.

quiz.q: Why is it important to feed at the same time each day?
options: B) To maintain rumen stability and prevent acidosis
quiz.explanation: Consistent feeding times keep rumen microbes stable and reduce the risk of acidosis.

quiz.q: What is the main benefit of using a feed mixer wagon with a scale?
options: B) It ensures accurate and uniform mixing
quiz.explanation: A mixer wagon with a scale accurately weighs and mixes ingredients, preventing sorting and errors.
